etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English veyn, from Old French vain, from Latin vānus (“empty”).

definitions.definition: Overly proud of oneself, especially concerning appearance; having a high opinion of one's own accomplishments with slight reason.

quote.citation: 1959, Leo Rosten, The return of H*Y*M*A*N K*A*P*L*A*N:
quote.text: Every writer is a narcissist. This does not mean that he is vain; it only means that he is hopelessly self-absorbed.

definitions.definition: Having no real substance, value, or importance; empty; void; worthless; unsatisfying.

quote.citation: c. 1590–1591 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Two Gentlemen of Verona”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene i]:
quote.text: I will not hear thy vain excuse

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Ephesians 5:6:
quote.text: Let no man deceive you with vain words.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book II”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: Vain wisdom all, and false philosophy.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “(please specify the book number)”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Vain is the force of man / To crush the pillars which the pile sustain.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto XXX, page 48:
quote.text: At our old pastimes in the hall⁠We gambol’d, making vain pretence⁠Of gladness, with an awful senseOf one mute Shadow watching all.

quote.citation: 1921, Ben Travers, chapter 6, in A Cuckoo in the Nest, Garden City, N.Y.: Doubleday, Page & Company, published 1925, →OCLC:
quote.text: But Sophia's mother was not the woman to brook defiance. After a few moments' vain remonstrance her husband complied. His manner and appearance were suggestive of a satiated sea-lion.

quote.citation: 1735, Alexander Pope, “Epistle 4”, in The Works of Mr. Alexander Pope, volume II, London:  […]  J. Wright, for Lawton Gilliver […], →OCLC, page 40, lines 25–30:
quote.text: Yet ſhall (my Lord) your juſt, your noble Rules / Fill half the land with imitating Fools: / VVho random dravvings from your ſheets ſhall take, / And of one beauty many blunders make; / Load ſome vain Church with old Theatric State, / Turn Arcs of Triumph to a Garden-gate,  […]

etymologies.etymologyHTML: A converstion of the adjectival form of vain. The only use of this verb in English appears c. 1628 in the writings of Owen Felltham.

definitions.definition: (transitive, rare, dated, obsolete) To frustrate. (The addition of quotations indicative of this usage is being sought:)
